question: What is the main job of the motor areas in the brain's cerebral cortex?

options.D: Processing visual images from the eyes

explanation: You've got this! The motor areas are specially designed to plan and make happen all the voluntary movements your body makes every day.

question: How do association areas differ from sensory and motor areas in the brain?

options.A: They directly connect spinal nerves to peripheral skeletal muscles
options.B: They are located exclusively deep within the brain stem rather than the cortex
options.C: They only function during deep sleep and remain completely inactive while awake
options.D: They deal with complex thoughts and reasoning rather than direct input or output

explanation: Think of association areas as the brain's processing hubs—they bring different pieces of information together for high-level thinking and reasoning!

question: Which specific lobe of the brain houses the primary motor cortex?
explanation: Great recall! The primary motor cortex lives right in the frontal lobe, specifically in the precentral gyrus.

question: Why does damage to the primary motor cortex on the right side of the brain cause weakness on the left side of the body?

options.A: The right side of the brain only controls internal organs
options.B: Motor pathways cross over to the opposite side of the body
options.C: Blood supply is shared equally between both body halves
options.D: Sensory nerves block motor signals from reaching the right limbs

explanation: Because of contralateral decussation, the motor cortex controls skeletal muscles on the opposite (contralateral) side of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h2)

question: What do we call the map-like representation of the body's muscles laid out across the motor cortex?
explanation: Spot on! The 'motor homunculus' is the quirky little brain map showing how cortical space is shared out among body parts.

question: Why do our hands and fingers take up such a huge chunk of space on the motor homunculus?

options.A: They require intricate, precise, and complex motor control
options.B: They have a much larger physical mass than the legs
options.C: They are closer to the brain than the lower extremities
options.D: They contain more bone density than other body parts

explanation: Makes total sense when you think about it—parts of the body that do delicate, skilled work (like typing or writing) get more brain real estate!

question: What is the main responsibility of the supplementary motor area (SMA)?

options.A: Regulating baseline heart rate and breathing
options.B: Processing sharp pain and temperature sensations
options.D: Translating spoken words into written text

explanation: You've got this! The SMA acts like a master planner, organizing movement sequences before you actually perform them.

question: A patient with an injury to their supplementary motor area would have the hardest time doing which of these?

options.A: Playing a practiced song on the piano from memory
options.B: Seeing a bright flashing light across the hospital room
options.C: Reflexively pulling a hand away from a hot stove burner
options.D: Feeling the texture of a piece of smooth velvet fabric

explanation: Playing an instrument takes smoothly linked, sequential movements—which is right up the SMA's alley!

question: Broca's area in the brain is mainly responsible for which function?
explanation: Fantastic! Broca's area coordinates your lips, tongue, and vocal cords so you can speak out loud clearly.

question: Which sign is most typical in a patient who has damage to Broca's area?

options.A: Inability to hear or recognize spoken words from others
options.B: Trouble speaking fluent words despite understanding language
options.C: Complete paralysis of all four limbs on the right side
options.D: Total loss of long-term memory about childhood events

explanation: This is expressive aphasia: the patient usually knows what they want to say in their head, but getting the words out is the struggle.

question: What is the primary role of the pyramidal motor tracts?

options.A: Transmitting pain signals from the feet

explanation: Spot on! Pyramidal tracts carry direct messages from the cortex for those precise, delicate movements we rely on.

question: How do extrapyramidal tracts differ from pyramidal tracts?

options.A: They control conscious decisions made during complex physical tasks
options.B: They regulate posture and muscle tone rather than fine voluntary skills
options.C: They carry nerve impulses exclusively upward toward the cerebral cortex
options.D: They cross over to the opposite side of the body at the midbrain level

explanation: You're crushing it! While pyramidal tracts handle fine skills, extrapyramidal pathways manage background posture and muscle tone.

question: What do we call weakness affecting one entire side of the body, often seen after a stroke?
explanation: You got it! 'Hemi' means half, and 'paresis' means weakness—a classic clinical term to remember for your exams and wards.

question: Why do patients with upper motor neuron injuries often develop tight, spastic muscles over time?

options.A: Loss of normal inhibitory control from higher brain centers
options.B: Permanent blockage of blood flow to the spinal nerves
options.C: Severe inflammation within the peripheral nerve endings
options.D: Direct destruction of the skeletal muscle fibers in the limbs

explanation: Think of upper motor neurons as holding the brakes. When they're damaged, those inhibitory brake signals are lost, leading to exaggerated reflexes and spasticity!
